original_title: Resident Evil Review: Zach Cregger Crafts an Ideal Tribute to an Iconic Series

en.title: Zach Cregger's Resident Evil Captures the Game's Terrifying Spirit
en.summary: Forget perfect lore adaptation; Zach Cregger's new film nails the feeling of playing Resident Evil. Austin Abrams stars as a hapless courier thrust into a nightmare.
en.body:
Few directors can blend intense horror with dark humor as effectively as **Zach Cregger**. His latest cinematic offering, a new take on the iconic **Resident Evil** franchise, isn't about slavishly recreating lore but about capturing the *feeling* of the games. Released in 2026 and clocking in at a lean 90 minutes, this film understands that the true terror of **Resident Evil** lies not just in its zombies, but in the pervasive sense of powerlessness and the desperate scramble for survival.

At the heart of this stripped-down, yet potent, vision is **Austin Abrams** as Bryan, a medical courier embodying the classic survival-horror protagonist. He's a gig worker, hurried and often ignored, just trying to get by. His ordinary day is violently upended when he accepts a lucrative, double-pay job to deliver a mysterious green case to Raccoon City. Cregger, along with co-writer **Shay Hatten**, expertly toys with audience expectations, drawing out the inevitable car crash with lingering shots of the road ahead, making the eventual impact all the more jarring. Abrams shines, seamlessly transitioning between tossing off witty one-liners and conveying sheer, unadulterated terror, much like **Ethan Winters** from **Resident Evil 7: Biohazard** and **Resident Evil Village**.

## The Everyman Against the Nightmare

Bryan's journey is a masterclass in building tension through relatable incompetence. His struggle with firearms, a running gag throughout the film, serves a dual purpose: it highlights his vulnerability and constantly reminds the audience of the razor-thin margin between survival and oblivion. Every fumbled reload and scarce bullet amplifies the dread, making his desperate fight against unimaginable horrors feel intensely personal. Cregger’s signature blend of dark humor, evident in his previous works like **Barbarian** and **Weapons**, remains a vital component, preventing the film from succumbing to relentless grimness and instead making Bryan's plight both terrifying and darkly amusing. The film perfectly encapsulates the experience of being thrown into a nightmarish scenario with impossible odds and dwindling resources.

## A Tribute to the Game's Soul

The **Resident Evil** franchise has always worn its cinematic influences on its sleeve, from the fixed camera angles of its earliest entries to the overt nods to films like *The Texas Chain Saw Massacre* in its later installments. Cregger’s film honors this legacy by understanding that the *spirit* of **Resident Evil** is more than just its monsters; it's the puzzle-solving under duress, the exploration of unsettling environments, and the feeling of being utterly outmatched. By focusing on an everyman protagonist navigating a hostile landscape, Cregger has crafted a tribute that resonates deeply with both long-time fans and newcomers, proving that sometimes, a lean, mean spin on the iconic horror formula is exactly what’s needed.

## What's Next

Fans eager to experience this intense new vision of **Resident Evil** can mark their calendars for its wide release on October 23, 2026. Further details regarding potential sequels or expanded lore are expected to be announced following the film's debut.

content_raw: Resident Evil , as a game series, has always borrowed heavily from cinema, whether it be the fixed angles and Kiyoshi Kurosawa inspirations of the first title to the Texas Chainsaw riffs in the 7th. It’s less about the zombies, more the feeling of powerlessness and weird puzzles. Zach Cregger understands this on a deep level. His follow-up to Weapons may not be a pitch-perfect adaptation of the long-running lore, but it perfectly captures the spirit of Resident Evil as a whole, not to mention what it’s like to play it. The perfect title might actually have been Biohazard .  Austin Abrams plays the classic survival-horror protagonist, which is to say: a person thrown into a situation with impossible odds, dwindling resources, and unimaginable horrors that test even hardened cops and soldiers. Bryan, a medical courier, is introduced in a long take amidst an argument on the phone with his girlfriend and blanching at a grizzly wound in the hospital. Like all gig workers, he’s hurried and ignored, ready to go home when presented with a job that’ll pay him double simply for taking a green case to Raccoon City. Who cares if his car has chains? Of course it goes wrong, but the greatest pleasure is how Cregger toys with audience expectations. He keeps cutting back from Bryan on the phone to the road ahead, drawing out the inevitable car crash until it happens with the victim in shallow focus. Barbarian and Weapons ‘ sense of humor retains throughout, Abrams once again making a great fit at both tossing off one-liners and being terrified. The RE protagonist he resembles the most—in tone and action, if not looks—is Ethan Winters, the lead of 7: Biohazard and 8: Village , a man who is just searching for his wife, has never used a gun before, and simply cannot believe any of this is happening. (When going under yet another tunnel, he says incredulously, “Who builds this shit?”) One of Resident Evil ’s best running gags is Bryan’s incompetence with firearms, but it also functions as a means of building tension. You’re always aware of how little ammo he has, and his frequent fumbles with reloading never get old. First and foremost, Resident Evil is a well-oiled scare machine from a director who already demonstrated proficiency with making the audience jump and laugh. This time he manages to get them doing both at once, and one doesn’t always know where they’ll end up. It helps that the monsters are inventively disgusting. Some may quibble with the fact that they’re not “traditional” zombies, to which I say: Resident Evil has always ended with some massively corrupted abomination against God and Science, not to mention changing what exactly the zombies are approximately every third entry. Rest assured that, despite them being relatively “new,” the multi-limbed crawler, claws, and tentacles are very faithful .
